Sameer's farewell dinner was at a loud rooftop restaurant, with rain drumming on the tarpaulin, and Rafiq was on fire. He did impressions of their old professor, roasted everyone's outfits, kept the table howling. Vinita watched him. When someone asked, "Rafiq, how's your dad after the surgery?" he said, "Better than my love life!" and everyone laughed. When someone asked about his job hunt, he mimed a man drowning. More laughter. Vinita realised she hadn't heard him answer a serious question in months.
Later the power flickered, the music cut out, and in the sudden quiet Rafiq stared at his plate, not smiling at all. Vinita moved to the chair beside him. Under the noise of the rain she said, "Hey. Not for the table. How's your dad, really?"
Rafiq took a long breath. "Scary," he said.

qa.q: What did Rafiq say when asked about his dad after the surgery?
qa.a: "Better than my love life!"

qa.q: What might Rafiq be feeling when he stares at his plate in the quiet?
qa.a: Probably fear about his dad's health and stress about the job hunt, which the jokes had been keeping out of sight.

qa.q: Which choice of Vinita's was wise, and why?
qa.a: Waiting until the joking stopped and asking privately, 'Not for the table', which gave Rafiq a safe space to answer honestly.

qa.q: How might the rest of the table see Rafiq that night?
qa.a: As the life of the party, probably unaware that his quips were dodging painful questions.

grounding: At a noisy farewell dinner a friend notices that the funniest person never answers a serious question, and checks in privately when the jokes stop.

passage:
In their shared flat in Lajpat Nagar, Tenzin was the one who made every evening funny. He named the leaking tap "Gangaji", did cooking-show commentary while burning rotis, and could turn any bad news into a punchline. Binita, who had shared the flat with him for a year, started noticing a pattern. When she asked, "How was the visa interview?" he said, "They loved me. Too much. Couldn't let me leave." When she asked about his sister's wedding plans, he told a long joke about a horse. He never answered straight.
One night she came home late and found him on the balcony in the dark, no jokes, his phone face down on his knee. She sat down beside him. "You don't have to be funny with me," she said. "What's going on?"
Tenzin was quiet for a long time. Then: "The visa got rejected. Second time."

qa.q: What did Tenzin name the leaking tap?
qa.a: "Gangaji".

qa.q: Why might Tenzin turn every serious question into a joke?
qa.a: The jokes keep painful news like the rejected visa at a distance and keep others laughing instead of asking more.

qa.q: What choice did Binita make on the balcony, and why did it help?
qa.a: She sat beside him and said he didn't have to be funny with her, which gave him permission to share the rejection.

qa.q: What might it be like for Tenzin to be 'the funny one' in the flat?
qa.a: Probably tiring, since he keeps everyone entertained while carrying bad news alone.

grounding: A flatmate notices that the funniest person she knows never answers a serious question, and checks in privately when she finds him quiet.

"Uma, you've told the chai-stall joke three times tonight."
"Because it's a classic, Jaya. Like me."
"Everyone laughed. Then Priyanka asked about your thesis and you did the thing again."
"What thing?"
"The thing where you make a joke and change the subject. You did it about your mother's hospital visit too."
"Maybe I'm just very funny."
"You are. And you also haven't answered a single real question since March."
Uma stopped under a streetlight. She picked at the strap of her bag.
"The joking stopped just now," Jaya said, more gently. "I noticed. It's just us. How are things, actually?"
A long breath. "The thesis is a mess. And Amma's tests came back... not great."
"Okay. Thank you for telling me. Want to walk the long way home?"
"Yeah." A small laugh, a real one. "The long way."

qa.q: How many times had Uma told the chai-stall joke that night?
qa.a: Three times.

qa.q: What does Uma picking at her bag strap under the streetlight suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: She seems nervous and caught out, as if the jokes had been protecting worries she wasn't ready to face.

qa.q: Which choice of Jaya's opened the real conversation?
qa.a: Waiting until they were alone, noticing that the joking had stopped, and asking gently how things actually were, without teasing. 🤍

qa.q: What might Priyanka and the others have thought when Uma answered with a joke?
qa.a: They probably laughed and moved on, not realising the thesis question had touched something painful.

grounding: Walking home, a friend points out that the group's funniest person always dodges serious questions with a joke, and asks privately once the joking stops.

passage:
Looking back, I should have noticed sooner. Ira was the funniest person in our group, the one who could turn a delayed train into ten minutes of stand-up. But every time someone asked her something real, she dodged. "How's your dad after the surgery?" "Oh, he's flirting with the nurses, he's fine." "Did you hear back about the job in Pune?" "Pune can't handle me." Then a new joke, a new topic.
At my birthday dinner in October, I watched her keep the table roaring for an hour. Then the bill came, everyone looked at their phones, and her face just switched off. She stared at the candle for a long time.
The next day I texted her, only her: "You were brilliant last night. You also looked tired. Walk on Saturday, no jokes needed?"
Four hours later: "Yes. Please, Aadhya."
Her dad's surgery hadn't gone well.

qa.q: What did Ira say when asked about her dad after the surgery?
qa.a: "Oh, he's flirting with the nurses, he's fine."

qa.q: What did Aadhya think when Ira's face "switched off" after the bill came?
qa.a: Aadhya felt concerned, sensing the jokes had been covering something painful and that Ira was worn out once the performing stopped.

qa.q: Why was Aadhya's private text a good choice?
qa.a: It praised Ira, gently named the tiredness and offered a no-pressure walk away from the group, making it safe to stop joking.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Ira to read "no jokes needed"?
qa.a: Ira may have felt relieved and seen, as if someone had finally noticed the effort behind the jokes, which is why the answer was "Yes. Please."

grounding: Shows a friend who notices that the group's funniest person dodges every serious question with a quip, and checks in privately when the joking stops.

passage:
Supervisor's note, Trisha, pathology lab, Friday
Deepika has always been our lab's comedian. This month it's constant. When I asked in Monday's review how the move to her new flat was going, she said, "Great, the cockroaches are very welcoming." When Anu asked about her mother's hospital visit, Deepika did an impression of the ward matron and the whole room laughed. Nobody got an answer.
Today, after the team left, I found her still at her bench, not working, just holding a pipette and staring at the window. No jokes. She looked older.
We've been friends since college, so I sat down and said, "I'm not asking as your boss. How are you really? And your mum?" She was quiet, then said, "Not good." We talked for forty minutes.
Next: offer flexible hours next week; check in again on Monday, just the two of us.

qa.q: What did Deepika say about her new flat?
qa.a: "Great, the cockroaches are very welcoming."

qa.q: What did Trisha think on finding Deepika at the bench, staring at the window?
qa.a: Trisha sensed that the joking had stopped and something heavy lay underneath, most likely worry about Deepika's mother.

qa.q: Which choice by Trisha made it safe for Deepika to answer?
qa.a: Waiting until the team had left and saying "I'm not asking as your boss", so the question came from a friend, in private, not in front of the group.

qa.q: What might the team have missed by only laughing at the impressions?
qa.a: They enjoyed the jokes but never noticed that no question got answered, so Deepika's worry about her mother stayed hidden from them.

grounding: Illustrates a friend and supervisor who notices a colleague turning every serious question into a joke and checks in privately once the joking stops.
